deep.reconstruction: Context (§§45–63 of E260). Euler models fluid 'friction' as a Coulomb-type wall resistance: on a tube element of length ds, cross-section gg and perimeter about 4g, the retarding force is α times the local pressure times the wall area. Pressure is measured as a height of water, and the atmosphere contributes l ≈ 30 ft of water. For a narrow vertical tube open at both ends and full of water, the weight of a slice is about gg·ds. The friction available is about α·(l + p)·g·ds. Constant factors are absorbed into α. At the critical state the inner pressure stays near l, so a slice cannot descend if g < αl, independent of tube length. §58 (previous page) turns this into a threshold: with α = 1/4000 and l = 30 ft, g < 0.0075 ft (diameter roughly a line). §59 (this page) gives the experiment. Fill tubes of different bore and find the widest one that no longer delivers a continuous stream; then α = g/l. Only a continuous stream (tractus continuus) counts as flow, not dripping. Euler's reason: friction acts only in true motion, so it cannot stop drops from slowly detaching under gravity. §60: the critical slenderness therefore depends on atmospheric pressure. In vacuo (l = 0) such tubes should empty completely, apart from the capillary column held by the 'nature proper to capillary tubes'. Water that only dripped in air would stream in vacuum. §61: in general atmospheric pressure, through pressure-proportional friction, always slows efflux (cf. §54: smaller l, faster jet). So any cause lowering the effective atmospheric pressure speeds efflux. Euler offers this as the explanation of the observed acceleration of water efflux by electricity (the electrified-capillary experiments of the 1740s, Nollet and others). §§62–63 (next page) show the same mechanism in the formula. With a closed top (f = 0), flow requires (1 − e^{−αb/g})·g/α > l, i.e. b > −(g/α)·log(1 − αl/g). This exponential saturation of wall-friction-controlled pressure is the Janssen-type law.
errors: Physically false premise: fluid wall friction is not proportional to normal pressure (Newtonian viscosity depends on velocity gradient). So the claimed dependence of the critical bore on atmospheric pressure, and the prediction that narrow tubes would stream in vacuo, are wrong. Retention of water in narrow open tubes is a surface-tension effect, independent of ambient pressure.

The criterion g < αl makes retention independent of tube length. Real capillary retention in an open vertical tube depends on column length relative to the capillary rise (roughly twice the rise height at most).

The electricity explanation (electrification lowering atmospheric pressure on the water) is unsupported. The real effect is electrohydrodynamic, from charge repulsion overcoming surface tension, as in electrospraying.
Minor, on the previous page §58: 'g > 3/400' should read 'g < 3/400', as the following 'seu g < 0,0075' shows. Also 'Si fuerit g = αl, seu g < αl' in §59 presumably means '≤'.

ideas.what: Static threshold for flow: a slender tube full of water cannot discharge if g < αl, because pressure-proportional wall friction exceeds the column weight; experimental determination α = g/l from the critical bore.
ideas.modern_name: Coulomb (pressure-proportional) wall friction leading to a jamming/plug threshold, as for granular plugs in pipes
ideas.usually_credited_to: Coulomb friction (Amontons 1699, Coulomb 1781); granular plug/silo wall friction (Janssen 1895)
ideas.where_published: E260 itself (Novi Comm. Petrop. 6, 1761); Opera omnia II.13 with Truesdell's commentary

ideas.what: Distinction between true flow (continuous stream) and dripping, since friction acts only in actual motion.
ideas.modern_name: static vs kinetic friction / dripping vs jetting transition
ideas.usually_credited_to: dripping–jetting transition studied in 19th–20th c. (Savart, Plateau, Rayleigh)

ideas.what: Prediction that narrow tubes that only drip in air would stream in vacuo.
Explanation of electrically accelerated efflux from capillaries as a reduction of atmospheric pressure acting through friction.
ideas.usually_credited_to: phenomenon: Bose, Nollet (1740s); theory: Rayleigh (1882), Zeleny (1914), Taylor (1964)
ideas.where_published: E260 §61; possibly related remarks in Euler's electricity writings (unsure)

missed.claim: Euler's fluid-friction model is formally the Janssen/Coulomb wall-friction model of granular media. This page states its threshold consequence: no flow from a slender tube when g < αl, and on the next page the exponential saturation 1 − e^{−αb/g}. The model is physically wrong for water but is exactly the silo/plug-jamming mechanics later developed for granular materials. The connection appears not to be noted in histories of granular mechanics.

missed.why_it_might_matter_today: This would place a 1761 derivation of a Janssen-type exponential and a frictional jamming criterion in a tube more than a century before Janssen (1895), which is of interest to historians of granular physics.

missed.claim: Euler gives an early mechanical (if wrong) explanation of electrically accelerated capillary efflux, a precursor phenomenon of electrospraying.

missed.why_it_might_matter_today: A minor footnote for the history of electrohydrodynamics; it shows the phenomenon was discussed by a leading theorist in 1761.

deep.surprise_reason: The physics is a known failed theory (pressure-proportional fluid friction), discussed in Opera omnia commentary. The structural identity with Coulomb/Janssen granular wall friction, including the jamming threshold and exponential saturation, is a plausible but modest unremarked connection. The electricity remark is a curiosity.
